speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I'm Dr. Agent. To help me determine the cause of your acute diarrhea, could you please tell me how long you have been experiencing these symptoms and describe the characteristics of the stool?

speaker: Patient
text: 58-year-old female. The patient has been treated for community-acquired pneumonia with levofloxacin on the medical floor. She reports developing watery diarrhea with at least 9 episodes within the last two days, accompanied by lower abdominal discomfort and cramping.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given your recent levofloxacin use, I am concerned about *Clostridioides difficile* infection. Have you experienced any fever or noticed blood or mucus in your stool?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Watery diarrhea. I also have Lower abdominal discomfort, Abdominal cramping.

speaker: Doctor
text: I need to confirm if you have had any fever or noticed blood or mucus in your stool, as this helps distinguish between simple antibiotic-associated diarrhea and a more serious infection. REQUEST TEST: C. difficile toxin assay

speaker: Doctor
text: Since the toxin assay result is inconclusive, I will order a more sensitive nucleic acid amplification test and a stool leukocyte count to look for inflammation. REQUEST TEST: C. difficile PCR; REQUEST TEST: Stool leukocytes

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the recent antibiotic use and high stool frequency, I suspect C. diff despite the initial negative tests, so I will order a CT scan of the abdomen to check for colitis. REQUEST TEST: CT abdomen

speaker: Doctor
text: Since the CT scan and stool tests are normal, C. difficile colitis is unlikely, suggesting this is likely uncomplicated antibiotic-associated diarrhea. I will discontinue the levofloxacin if clinically appropriate and initiate supportive care with oral rehydration and symptom management. DIAGNOSIS READY: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea
